strengths: Very large-scale, systematic empirical study spanning 14 open-source models (2B-72B) plus GPT-4o, 3 domains (math, knowledge, NL reasoning), and 12 benchmarks, enabling robust cross-model and cross-domain generalization claims.

Well-designed controlled experiments that carefully isolate three factors (problem difficulty, generator capability, verifier capability) with sensible methodological controls, e.g., balanced TPR/TNR subsampling, filtering for fair generator comparisons, and repeated randomized subsampling to reduce bias.

The stratified analysis of verifier capability vs. verification accuracy (Section 4.3) revealing regime-dependent (saturated/linear/threshold) relationships is a genuinely useful refinement over prior work that only reported a global linear correlation.

Clear translation of the descriptive findings into actionable implications for test-time scaling, including quantified gap-closing results (e.g., 75.5% Gemma2-9B/27B gap reduction) and identification of regimes where scaling verifiers provides no benefit.

Illustrative case studies (Figures 18-19) provide plausible qualitative mechanisms (verifier self-generated reference errors driving false negatives; strong generators' internally consistent errors evading detection) that add interpretability beyond pure correlation.
Extensive appendix material, including generalization checks to reasoning/thinking models, strengthens robustness of the main claims.
weaknesses: The core findings are largely confirmatory/incremental extensions of well-established intuitions (easier problems are easier to verify; weak generators make more obviously wrong answers; stronger verifiers tend to verify better) rather than surprising or mechanistically novel insights; the primary contribution is more a large replication/stratification study than a new conceptual or methodological advance.

The analysis is purely observational/correlational; no causal interventions (e.g., controlled error injection, prompting ablations, or training a verifier) are used to establish that the identified factors are truly causal drivers versus confounded byproducts of how problems/models were selected.

The problem-difficulty metric d(x) is defined as the average pass rate across the same set of models used later as generators/verifiers, creating potential circularity/leakage between the independent variable and outcome metrics.

TTS formulation uses an unconventional 'expected pass rate of retained pool' rather than standard Best-of-N/majority-vote selection used in most prior TTS work, limiting direct comparability of the reported gains to the broader literature the paper positions itself against.

Verification is evaluated only via single-prompt, generic zero-shot CoT + verdict verifiers; the paper does not compare against trained/specialized verifiers, ensembles, or alternative verification strategies (self-consistency, majority voting among verifiers) that are common in practice, which limits the generality of conclusions about 'verifier scaling.'

No statistical significance testing or confidence intervals are reported for the many correlation/R² values and gap-closing percentages, making it hard to assess robustness of quantitative claims across the large parameter sweep.

The explanatory case studies, while illustrative, are anecdotal (a handful of examples) rather than systematically quantified, so the proposed mechanisms (e.g., verifiers generating their own reference solutions) are not rigorously validated at scale.

strengths: Extremely comprehensive empirical study spanning 14 open-source models plus GPT-4o (2B-72B+), 3 domains (math, knowledge, NL reasoning), and 12 benchmarks, providing a large and diverse evidence base.

Novel and useful disentanglement of three factors (problem difficulty, generator capability, verifier generation capability) that jointly determine verification success, rather than treating verification quality as a single scalar tied only to verifier strength.

Findings have direct, actionable implications for test-time scaling (e.g., weak generators can approach strong-generator TTS performance when paired with a good verifier; strong verifiers sometimes offer negligible benefit), which is practically valuable for reducing inference cost.

Strong effort toward mechanistic explanation: large-scale LLM-as-judge analyses (with bootstrapped CIs) linking false negatives to faulty self-generated reference solutions, and linking TNR decline to increasingly coherent/subtle errors from strong generators, supported by illustrative case studies.

Extensive robustness checks: reasoning models (Qwen3-Thinking), very large models (Qwen3-235B), multiple verification prompt templates, and an alternative label-free difficulty estimator, all showing consistent trends.

Good reproducibility practices: full prompt templates, metric definitions, model naming tables, and an efficiency analysis (FLOPs) translating findings into concrete cost/performance guidance for generator/verifier selection.
weaknesses: The high-level qualitative conclusions (verification correlates with problem difficulty, generator strength, and verifier capability) are not deeply surprising; the contribution is primarily in the fine-grained characterization (regimes, curve shapes) rather than a fundamentally new phenomenon, and overlaps with concurrent work (Lu et al. 2025) that the authors acknowledge but only briefly contrast.

The interpretability analyses (solving-mistake detection, surface-level error classification) rely entirely on LLM-as-judge (GPT-4.1-mini) without human validation, raising concern about the reliability of the causal explanations offered for the main findings.

Problem difficulty is defined as the average pass rate across the same pool of generator models used elsewhere in the study, which risks some circularity when relating difficulty to generator/verifier capability effects.

The stratification thresholds used to define 'hard/medium/easy' regimes for RQ3 (and similarly the difficulty quartiles) appear somewhat ad hoc, and results could be sensitive to the specific binning/threshold choices, which is not stress-tested against alternative binning schemes.

The TTS metric (expected pass rate of the verifier-retained pool) explicitly diverges from the standard best-of-N/majority-vote selection paradigm used in most prior work, which may limit direct comparability with existing TTS literature despite some majority-vote results being reported in appendix.

Verifier 'generation capability' is measured by prompting the verifier itself as a generator on the same problem set, which is a reasonable but imperfect proxy for the skills actually needed for verification (e.g., error-detection versus solving from scratch), potentially conflating two related but distinct capacities.
The paper is very dense, with the bulk of quantitative depth and many robustness results relegated to a lengthy appendix, making it harder to assess the core claims from the main text alone.
